title: Which favors will you deny?
hook: the refrain repeated thirty-one times: which of your Lord's favors will you deny (55:13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mizan, and your line was keep the balance. Did you make your one small correction? Day six hundred five.

If you've ever heard Surah Ar-Rahman recited out loud, you know the moment. A few verses go by, describing fruit, or the seas, or the rising places of the sun. And then the same line comes back, with the same melody, and the listener starts waiting for it. It comes again. And again. By the end of the surah, it has returned thirty-one times. A child who knows nothing else of the surah can usually sing that one line. Today, the question that keeps coming back.

Verse thirteen, the first time it appears. Pickthall: "Which is it, of the favours of your Lord, that ye deny?" In Arabic: fa-bi-ayyi ala'i rabbikuma tukadhdhiban. Two things are hidden in the grammar. First, rabbikuma, your Lord, and tukadhdhiban, you deny, are dual: they speak to two. Who are the two? Later in the surah, verse thirty-three addresses the company of jinn and humans, and commentators read the whole refrain as spoken to both. Second, ala'. Pickthall says favors, and that is the usual reading: blessings, bounties, gifts. Some commentators add that ala' can also carry the sense of wonders, signs of power. So the line asks two things at once: which of these gifts, and which of these marvels, will you call a lie? Notice that it's a question, not an accusation. The surah lists a gift, then stops and asks. Fruit and palm trees: which will you deny? The two seas and their pearls: which will you deny? Even warnings get the refrain, as if being warned were a kindness too. A report in Tirmidhi's collection tells that the Prophet ﷺ once recited this surah to his companions, who listened in silence. He told them the jinn had answered it better: each time he reached the refrain, they replied that they denied none of their Lord's favors, and praise belonged to Him. Many Muslims still answer the refrain under their breath when they hear it. The repetition isn't filler. It's the surah teaching you to stop after every blessing and notice it.
screen: `FA-BI-AYYI ALA'I RABBIKUMA.` · `SPOKEN TO TWO: JINN AND HUMANS.` · `A QUESTION, NOT AN ACCUSATION.` · `THE JINN ANSWERED IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: say it after each blessing you notice. Sit, and breathe. Let one ordinary gift come to mind: the breath you're taking, the light in the room, someone who texted you this week. After each one, ask the question quietly: which of His favors? If you pray, you can answer the way many Muslims do, that you deny none of them. If you don't, simply name the gift and let it sit. Then the next one. The bell holds the time.
Which favors will you deny? The refrain of Surah Ar-Rahman, asked thirty-one times, to jinn and humans alike. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: which of his favors? Today, three times, when something good happens, ask it under your breath before you move on. Day six hundred five.
